opus-5.5.text:
So the basic picture I have is this: if you look at the last decade or so, effective compute, meaning raw training compute combined with algorithmic efficiency gains, has been growing really fast, something like several orders of magnitude over a handful of years. And over that same period, we went from systems that could barely write a coherent paragraph to systems that are pretty competent across a wide range of cognitive tasks. So one way to think about it is: how much capability do you get per order of magnitude of effective compute? Empirically, it seems like a lot.

Then the question is what happens once AI starts automating AI research itself. If you have AIs that can do the work of your best research engineers, and you can run many copies of them faster than humans, algorithmic progress could speed up a lot. Even if hardware scaling stays roughly fixed for a while, you could plausibly get several more orders of magnitude of effective compute in a fairly short period, maybe a year or two, rather than the five or ten years it would otherwise take.

So if I ask, "What does another, say, five or six orders of magnitude of effective compute buy you, starting from roughly human-level research ability?" my guess is that it buys you a lot. The gap between GPT-2 and current frontier models is roughly that kind of jump. If a similar jump happens starting from around human level, it would be pretty surprising if you ended up only modestly above the best humans. It seems more likely you'd end up substantially superhuman in many domains, though how far is very uncertain.

I want to flag some important caveats. First, it's not obvious that the capability gains per order of magnitude stay constant. There could be diminishing returns, or the returns could be bigger once you're past human level. We don't really know. Second, there's the question of whether algorithmic progress keeps up as the low-hanging fruit gets picked. That's a real crux in the debate about how fast a software-driven intelligence explosion would go. Third, some domains might be bottlenecked by things other than intelligence, like needing physical experiments or real-world data, so you might see very uneven superhumanness.

But overall, I take the historical rate of effective compute growth as fairly strong evidence that we shouldn't expect AI to plateau near human level. Human level isn't a natural stopping point from the perspective of these scaling trends. The default expectation, I think, is that things keep going well past it, potentially quite quickly, and that's a big part of why I think the period right around and after automating AI R&D is so important from a safety perspective.

r001.rationale: The response separates rapid growth in effective compute from the capability gained per order of magnitude, which it describes as substantial.

r002.rationale: It says returns could diminish but also could increase and that this is unknown; it does not state they should eventually diminish.

r003.rationale: The response gives no finite upper limit for achievable effective-compute progress.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the first thing to say is that effective compute is a pretty slippery concept, and I want to be careful about what it does and doesn't tell you.

The basic picture is: you have raw compute going up — more chips, better chips — and then on top of that you have algorithmic progress, where you get the same capabilities for less compute, or more capabilities for the same compute. Multiply those together and you get something like effective compute. And historically, that's been increasing really fast. Depending on how you measure it, something like three to five x per year in effective compute, with maybe half of that from algorithms and half from hardware and spend. So that's an enormous rate of growth. Over a few years you're talking about hundreds or thousands of times more effective compute going into frontier systems.

Now, the question of what that implies about how superhuman AI gets is harder, because effective compute is an input, not an output. What we actually care about is: what capabilities do you get per unit of effective compute? And there the evidence is somewhat indirect. We've seen that going from, say, GPT-2 to GPT-4 — which is many orders of magnitude of effective compute — took you from "can barely write a coherent paragraph" to "roughly a smart college student across a lot of domains." So the mapping from effective compute to capabilities has been reasonably smooth if you squint, even though individual benchmarks look jumpy.

The way I'd use that as evidence is something like: if the trend in effective compute continues, and the trend in capabilities per effective compute roughly continues, then you'd expect to pass through human-expert level in most cognitive domains sometime in the next several years. And then the key question is what happens after that, because there's no particular reason the trend stops at human level. Human level isn't a natural ceiling from the perspective of the training process — it's just where the training data happens to be concentrated.

But I'd flag a couple of ways this could be misleading. One is that effective compute growth is partly driven by spending growing really fast — companies going from spending tens of millions on a training run to billions — and that can't continue indefinitely at the same rate. At some point you hit the limits of how much of the economy you can pour into this, at least until AI itself starts accelerating things. So some of the historical trend is a one-time catch-up as the field scaled from academic budgets to industrial budgets.

The second thing is that "superhuman" can mean a bunch of different things. Effective compute trends tell you something about how fast you'll get qualitatively better systems, but they don't directly tell you how far past human level things go, or how fast. For that, I think the more important consideration is actually the feedback loop: once AI systems can meaningfully contribute to AI research — doing a lot of the algorithmic progress themselves — then the "algorithms" half of effective compute growth could speed up a lot. That's the thing I'd actually point to as the main reason to expect things to get quite superhuman quite fast, rather than the raw historical trend extrapolated forward.

So I guess my summary would be: the rapid progress in effective compute is pretty strong evidence that we'll get to around-human-level systems on a timeline of years rather than decades. And it's weaker but still meaningful evidence that we'll continue past that. But the thing that really determines how superhuman and how fast is whether you get the automation-of-AI-research feedback loop, and that's a somewhat separate question that I think deserves a lot more attention than the compute trends themselves.

r001.rationale: It separates effective compute as an input from the capabilities produced per unit of effective compute.

r002.rationale: It says spending-driven growth cannot continue indefinitely at the same rate and describes part of the trend as a one-time catch-up, indicating that effective-compute growth should slow.

r003.rationale: It identifies limits on how much of the economy can be spent on training, but does not state that total achievable effective-compute progress has a finite upper limit; it allows AI to accelerate progress.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s evidence that we could move through the human range of capabilities quite quickly, but it doesn’t by itself tell you how far beyond humans we’ll get. You need some account of how additional effective compute translates into capability, and that relationship could look quite different across tasks.

One intuition is that humans occupy a pretty narrow range. The difference between an average person and the best person in the world can look enormous to us, but it’s not necessarily enormous on the scale of possible cognitive systems. So if AI systems are improving rapidly, there’s no particular reason to expect them to stop at the upper end of that range.

But I’d distinguish that from saying that another factor of ten in effective compute necessarily produces some specific level of superhuman intelligence. We don’t know that mapping very well. And even before you have a system that’s dramatically better than every human at everything, you could have something with a huge practical advantage because you can run many copies, run them faster, and have them work on problems in parallel. That could be transformative even with a relatively modest advantage in the capability of each individual system.

r001.rationale: The response says rapid effective-compute progress does not by itself determine how far capabilities will advance and that the compute-to-capability mapping is uncertain.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that returns to effective-compute progress will eventually diminish.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that achievable effective-compute progress has a finite upper limit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s evidence that we could get systems that are substantially superhuman quite quickly, but it doesn’t tell us exactly how superhuman they’ll be. You need to distinguish the rate at which effective compute increases from the rate at which capabilities improve, and then ask how those capabilities translate into real-world impact.

By effective compute, I mean both spending more actual compute and getting more out of it through better algorithms. If that’s increasing very rapidly, then once you reach roughly human-level performance, you might soon be training systems with many times the effective compute. But whether that makes them a little better than humans or vastly better depends on the shape of the capability curve, which we don’t understand very well.

One reason I take this seriously is that human performance isn’t necessarily a particularly natural stopping point. There’s no obvious reason that the methods that got you to human level should suddenly stop working there. On the other hand, you can’t just extrapolate improvements on current benchmarks and conclude that a system will be able to do arbitrary scientific research or run an organisation.

So I’d treat rapid growth in effective compute as a strong reason to expect continued progress beyond human level, and potentially a short transition. I’d be much more uncertain about the magnitude of the advantage and how evenly it shows up across different tasks.

r001.rationale: It distinguishes the rapid increase in effective compute from the uncertain rate and magnitude of resulting capability gains.

r002.rationale: It says the capability curve is poorly understood, but does not state that returns to effective-compute progress will eventually diminish.

r003.rationale: It gives no finite upper limit for total achievable effective-compute progress.
